PHSCS 587

MOS C–V and response time

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows why one MOS structure can produce low-frequency, high-frequency and deep-depletion curves

A capacitance measurement asks how much gate charge changes for a small voltage change around a DC bias. Per unit area, C′ = dQg′/dVg and Cox′ = εox/tox. In an ideal MOS capacitor with a conductive gate, oxide and semiconductor differential capacitances are in series: 1/C′ = 1/Cox′ + 1/Cs′. Cs′ represents the semiconductor charge response, including whichever mobile and depletion components can follow the measurement.

At one bias point, the depletion and inversion charge responses share the same surface-potential change, so their differential contributions add within Cs′ when each population can respond. The oxide and that combined semiconductor response carry equal incremental gate charge in the ideal series description. This explains why the inversion response can change with frequency while the physical oxide capacitance stays the same.

For a p-type body, accumulation commonly gives C′ near Cox′. Depletion widens a space-charge region and lowers C′. In strong inversion with a sufficiently slow small signal and an available minority-carrier supply, inversion charge follows and capacitance rises toward Cox′. At high small-signal frequency the minority population cannot change appreciably, so the measured capacitance stays near the series combination with the maximum-depletion capacitance Cdep,max′ = εs/Wmax.

The DC sweep rate is a second timescale. A rapid move into inversion can leave too few minority carriers to establish the equilibrium inversion layer, extending depletion beyond Wmax and reducing capacitance below its high-frequency equilibrium minimum: deep depletion. Interface traps, series resistance and contact geometry add further responses. Always state bias history, AC frequency and how minority carriers are supplied when interpreting C–V.

Example

Suppose a depletion-region semiconductor capacitance is equal to Cox′. Their series combination is C′ = Cox′/2. A later low-frequency inversion response can raise Cs′ substantially and move the measured C′ back toward Cox′.

Practice

1. How do high-frequency inversion and deep depletion differ physically?

Separate a small AC perturbation from the establishment of the DC carrier population.

High-frequency equilibrium inversion has a DC inversion population that cannot follow the fast AC signal. Deep depletion lacks enough inversion charge even for the evolving DC bias, so depletion extends farther.

2. Why can oxide capacitance stay unchanged while measured MOS capacitance falls?

Include the semiconductor component.

The oxide remains the same, while a smaller semiconductor differential capacitance reduces the series total.
